Dr. Shangrila Joshi Scholar & author Patan, Nepal - Olympia, WA

Who governs the commons decides who weathers the crisis.

( The research )

Shangrila Joshi studies the shared resources we all depend on - the atmosphere, the forests - and asks who gets to govern them. She examines how climate change is governed, who carries its costs, and how communities defend the shared resources - the atmosphere, forests, and water - that climate policy so often treats as commodities. Her work moves between global negotiation rooms and village forest committees. She is faculty in the Master of Environmental Studies program at The Evergreen State College, and a Newar scholar, part of the Indigenous Nationality of Nepal.

( The work )

The atmosphere and the forests are a commons - shared by everyone, owned by no one. Her research follows that question from the treaty rooms of Copenhagen to the community forests of Nepal and the festival streets of the Kathmandu Valley.

( Research in full )

Three connected lines of inquiry run through the work: how the global commons is governed, how market-based climate solutions land in particular places, and how Indigenous institutions sustain resilience over centuries.

01

Climate justice and the global commons

An analysis of North-South inequities in responsibility, vulnerability, and capability, traced through global climate treaty negotiations from Rio to Paris. The atmosphere and the world’s forests are treated as resource commons, and the central question is a justice question: how ideas of injustice pertaining to colonialism, race, Indigeneity, caste, gender, and global inequality intersect with the politics of scale.

02

Market mechanisms in Nepal

A critical examination of the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation) as they have been implemented within Nepal, with an eye towards understanding their implications for sustainable community forest governance and how they transform social relations around the forest commons in the places where they land.

03

Indigenous knowledge and resilience

The current book project: the Newa Guthi, the traditional institution that sustains festivals such as the Machchhindra Nath Jatra in the Kathmandu Valley, studied as a living system of governance. Recent writing brings the Newa literary tradition of the Swasthani Vrata Katha into conversation with the festival tradition to argue for an Indigenous climate epistemology.

02 - The book, Routledge - 2021 - 236 pages

Climate Change Justice and Global Resource Commons

Local and Global Postcolonial Political Ecologies

This book examines the multiple scales at which the inequities of climate change are borne out. It engages in a multi-scalar analysis of the myriad ways in which various resource commons - predominantly atmosphere and forests - are implicated in climate governance, with a consistent emphasis throughout on the justice implications for disenfranchised communities.

Drawing on qualitative interviews conducted in Delhi, Kathmandu, and the Terai region of Nepal, participant observation at the Climate Conference in Copenhagen (COP-15), and textual analysis of official documents, the book articulates a geography of climate justice. It will be of interest to students and scholars of environmental justice, climate justice, climate policy, political ecology, and South Asian studies.

The book has been taken up in review forums including The AAG Review of Books (2024), where scholars including Dinesh Paudel, Bill Derman, Galen Murton, and Costanza Rampini discussed it alongside Dr. Joshi, and a companion forum on struggles for climate justice with Tracy Osborne, Patrick Bond, Zoltán Grossman, and Jennifer Rice.

The book was also reviewed by Tariro Kamuti in the International Journal of Environmental Studies (2022).

Current project - The second book

The Newa Guthi
and the Jatra

The second book turns from global negotiation rooms to one of the oldest continuously sustained institutions in the Kathmandu Valley, and asks what it can teach climate policy about resilience.

The Guthi is the traditional Newa institution through which land, labor, ritual, and care for shared places have been organized for centuries. Among the traditions it sustains is the Machchhindra Nath Jatra, the chariot festival of the rain deity, whose timing and procession are bound up with the monsoon and with the agricultural life of the valley.

The book draws on a two-year ethnographic study of the Jatra. On May 24, 2025, Dr. Joshi organized a multi-stakeholder forum in Nepal, “The Significance of the Machchhindranath Jatra and the Newa Guthi for Climate Adaptation in Nepal,” preceded by two half-day workshops and attended by over 150 participants in all, bringing together traditional practitioners, cultural experts, and climate policy decision-makers. The argument running through the project is that Indigenous traditions like these are not folklore to be preserved alongside climate policy, but working systems of governance that climate adaptation efforts need to include in a meaningful way.

In 2024, the Rubin Museum of Himalayan Art awarded her a $10,000 Rubin x Research grant for “Arts of Resilience: Lessons from the Machchhindranath Jatra of Patan,” supporting the in-depth ethnography behind the book.

06 - The person

Really her

A short version. The full story lives in the book and the talks.

From Patan to Olympia, following one question the whole way.

“I am a core member of the Master of Environmental Studies program at Evergreen,” Dr. Joshi writes. “My scholarship examines the human dimensions of global climate change, with a focus on environmental and climate justice, and institutions of commons governance.”

Shangrila Joshi is a Newar scholar, part of the Indigenous Nationality of Nepal, born in Patan (Lalitpur) in the Kathmandu Valley. Her degrees run from St. Xavier’s College in Kathmandu to Ohio University and a PhD at the University of Oregon, where her dissertation took on North-South climate politics around COP-15 in Copenhagen. Her first book examined climate policy and politics within a multi-scalar political ecology framework, centered on the Kyoto Protocol and market-based climate solutions. She has contributed book chapters to Climate, Science, and Society: A Primer, the Handbook of Global Environmental Politics, and The International Handbook of Political Ecology, and her journal work includes Global Environmental Politics (2013) and Critical Humanities (2025).

As of 2021, she had spent an equal number of years in Nepal and in the United States - a biographical fact that sits underneath a body of work preoccupied with North-South relations, colonial history, and who gets to define a climate solution.

After visiting posts at Denison, Colgate, and Temple, she accepted a tenure-track position at The Evergreen State College, where she now teaches in the Master of Environmental Studies program and in undergraduate climate justice. Her current book project returns home: the Newa Guthi institutions and the Machchhindra Nath Jatra, read as a living system of climate resilience.

She received a Sylff fellowship at the University of Oregon in 2008, and has twice led Sylff Leaders Initiative forums - on climate justice and REDD+ in 2019, and in May 2025 on the significance of the Machchhindranath Jatra and the Newa Guthi for climate adaptation in Nepal, a forum that drew the attention of Nepalese decision-makers on climate policy in government and non-governmental organizations alike. In 2024 she received a Rubin Museum research grant to complete an in-depth ethnography of the Machchhindra Nath Jatra, and in 2025 she was named a Storymakers Fellow by the USC Wrigley Institute for Environment and Sustainability.

07 - Teaching

Teaching at Evergreen

Core faculty in Evergreen’s Master of Environmental Studies program, with undergraduate teaching in climate justice.

( Teaching philosophy )

“Environmental problems tend to be complex and their solutions controversial; therefore, inculcating habits of learning across significant differences is critical. My approach to teaching typically involves introducing multiple perspectives when examining a particular subject.”

Her teaching draws on Evergreen’s framework of interdisciplinary teaching and learning to bring together multiple ideas and perspectives - natural sciences, social sciences, traditional ecological knowledge, public policy, and environmental humanities.

“My role as teacher is to help students navigate the complex and often conflicted terrain of ideas on how best to address environmental challenges, as well as to help them develop nuanced understandings and articulate their ideas with precision.”Shangrila Joshi, on her teaching, via The Evergreen State College
